# Which coding-agent CLI is best for headless workflow automation?

Bulat Â· Co-authored with AI Â· 21 October 2026

A coding-agent CLI can feel quick in a terminal and still be expensive when a workflow starts it in a fresh container for every job. We measured that cost for six CLIs: start-up, time per turn, memory, image size and tokens.

On overhead per job, pi was the lightest overall. Our own CLI, aictrl , won no metric but came second on four: session time, harness time per turn, memory and image size. Overhead is half the answer: this experiment does not measure whether an agent completes the task, which our next run will.

Goose had the fastest observed median first response, followed by Codex, pi and aictrl. Those four were within 187 ms of each other. pi used the fewest tokens, both in its first request and for a whole short task, spent the least time between model turns, added the least image footprint and finished the scripted session fastest. aictrl came second on session time, per-turn harness time, memory and image footprint. Its system prompt is now as small as pi's. Its tool definitions are not.

Each chart is sorted from lowest to highest, with gold and silver medals for the observed first and second place on that metric. A medal describes this experiment; small gaps do not establish a stable lead.

Disclosure: I build aictrl. This article reports our own measurements, including where our implementation loses. The article and charts were prepared with AI assistance.

## What we measured

On 20 October 2026 we tested released installations of aictrl 0.5.4, pi 1.3.0, Codex 0.163.0, OpenCode 2.1.0, Hermes Agent v0.22.2 source and Goose 1.55.0. Hermes' source archive reports vunknown ; we identify it by its pinned release commit in the methodology .

Every attempt started a fresh non-root container with an empty home directory, a two-CPU quota and a 2 GiB memory limit. Images were already on the host, and filesystem caches were not cleared. These are fresh-container measurements, excluding image downloads and cloud scheduling.

A local scripted model responded after a fixed 50 ms delay. It removed remote inference variability and dictated the reads. This tests harness overhead and native tool execution; it cannot measure coding quality or natural model-turn efficiency.

For the architectural context behind these measurements, read our agent framework comparison . It examines the framework and harness choices to consider alongside per-job overhead.

We collected 20 measured single-response attempts per harness and five attempts for the 50-read memory task, with two discarded warmups per scenario and interleaved harness order. All six used their own native tool loops. Hermes did not delegate to Codex, and Goose did not delegate through ACP. Every attempt completed, and the runner recorded no failures.

The toolsets were not equal, and that matters most for the token results. pi ran with its four default tools, no subagent tool and no extensions or packages installed. Goose ran with only its built-in Developer extension, so no recipes or sub-recipes were loaded. Hermes ran with only its file and terminal toolsets; its default also enables web, browser, memory and task delegation, among others. aictrl, OpenCode and Codex ran with their default tools, which include a subagent tool in each. The section on tokens adds aictrl restricted to pi's four tools.

Each harness ran non-interactively with its JSON output on. Besides the scripted model's provider settings, the flags were:

- aictrl: aictrl run --format json

- pi: pi --mode json

- Codex: codex exec --json --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --skip-git-repo-check

- OpenCode: opencode run --standalone --auto --format json

- Goose: goose run --no-profile --with-builtin developer --output-format stream-json

- Hermes: hermes chat --oneshot --toolsets file,terminal --ignore-user-config --ignore-rules --format stream-json

The runner has the full adapters, environment and config files.

For token counts we ran a separate capture campaign with the same images and setup. It used five single-response and five 50-read sessions per harness and retained every request body. We counted every harness with one reference tokenizer, OpenAI's o200k_base . These are estimates of what each harness sends, not provider-billed usage.

The measurement extract , token estimates , CSV and methodology accompany the figures. Memory and footprint use MiB; request bodies use actual UTF-8 bytes. Select any chart to open the full-resolution image.

## Goose had the fastest observed median first response

The timer started immediately before docker run and stopped at the first matching assistant-response event in the harness's JSON output. Container startup and our setup wrapper count. This is not model time to first token.

Goose reached the first response in 392 ms at the median, followed by Codex at 471, pi at 522 and aictrl at 579. With 20 samples on a shared host, I would not claim a repeatable ordering among those four. Absolute startup times also moved between our campaigns: the same Goose, Codex, pi and Hermes images measured 140 to 230 ms faster on 20 October than a day earlier. A separate paired run of aictrl and pi measured 503 and 460 ms. Compare startup times within one campaign only. OpenCode 2.1.0 took 926 ms and Hermes 5.5 s, gaps that warrant profiling under the same setup.

These are supported installation profiles with different runtimes, dependencies and startup behavior. pi used Node 22; Hermes core used Python 3.14.8. The other three npm installations used a Node 20 base, while packaged native executables can carry their own runtime. Those differences prevent attributing the result to a programming language.

## Memory depends on what reaches the next model request

The long task read fifty distinct files containing the same 48,000-byte, 800-line fixture, then answered Done. . Distinct paths matter: Hermes normally deduplicates unchanged reads. We preserved that behavior while asking each harness to do actual reads of equal-sized files.

All six completed all five attempts. pi had the lowest median cgroup peak at 154 MiB, followed by aictrl at 207. Codex measured 132 MiB, but it did not hold the same data. Its shell tool cuts long output: of each 800-line file the model saw lines 1â84 and 718â800, with a note that 38,000 characters were removed. That is about a fifth of the file.

The final request was 572,750 bytes for Codex versus 2.46â2.67 million bytes for the others. The validator classified all five Codex runs as shortened context; every other harness delivered and retained complete fixture content in all five attempts. A smaller context is cheaper, but an agent reviewing a long file never sees its middle.

Cgroup memory includes charged cache. Shared host page-cache ownership can change which container bears that cost. Largest-process RSS and sampled summed RSS are also retained in the data; they measure different quantities. A low cgroup reading alone does not mean the process resident set is equally small.

We verify source-line coverage in the next model request and check every result again in the final request. Codex's native output cap yields a much smaller final request. Its memory result therefore cannot establish that it stores an equivalent conversation more efficiently. The stub also reports artificial usage, so normal token-driven context compaction is not exercised.

## Turnaround: where the session time goes

Each session made 51 main model calls: fifty tool-call responses and a final answer. OpenCode and Hermes each made one additional auxiliary model call. The script imposes the main-call count, so this experiment cannot show how many turns a harness would take on a real task.

It can show what each harness adds to every turn. The stub timestamps each request and response, so we split the session into start-up, time waiting for the model, harness work between turns and shut-down.

The model wait was about 3 s for everyone: 51 calls at 50 ms plus serialization. The difference is harness work. Between turns pi took a median 9 ms and aictrl 12 ms. OpenCode took 32 ms, Codex 45, Hermes 64 and Goose 72. Codex and Goose run each read as a shell cat , which starts a process. The other four use a native file reader.

Summed over a session, the gaps came to a median 0.5 s for pi, 0.6 s for aictrl and 3.8 s for Goose, whose slower turns also vary more. With a real model taking seconds per turn they are a small share of the total. The turn count, which a real model decides, is the larger lever. Hermes also spent 5.3 s before its first request and 1 s shutting down.

## OpenCode's npm installation was the largest

npm installed four Linux x64 binaries for OpenCode 2.1.0: glibc and musl builds, each in a regular and a baseline variant. Each takes about 204 MiB, and the launcher uses one. Its platform packages declare the operating system and CPU but not the C library, so npm cannot skip the variants this host does not need.

aictrl's platform packages declare their C library, so npm installs only the one binary the host needs. It adds 113 MiB, about 6 MiB more than pi. The build metadata records the installed packages.

We did not measure image pulls, so the experiment identifies duplication without quantifying its deployment-time penalty.

## Tokens: fixed cost per call, then what the read tool returns

Every call resends the system prompt and the tool definitions, so their size is a fixed cost on each turn. We split the first request into those two parts and the rest: the task message, any context the harness injects, and JSON framing.

aictrl's system prompt is 608 tokens, level with pi's 601 and Goose's 563. The remaining gap to pi is the tool definitions: nine tools at 2,772 tokens against pi's four at 609. Our read tool alone is described in 394 tokens, pi's in 159.

Most of that gap is a design choice about which tools to declare. pi declares four by default and leaves out subagents on purpose. Its README says it "skips features like sub-agents and plan mode", and offers subagents as an optional extension that runs each one as a separate process. Search goes through bash . aictrl also declares glob , grep , webfetch , a skill loader, and a task tool that starts subagents. Those five add about 1,350 tokens to every call. OpenCode's twelve tools include a subagent tool too.

For workflow automation, that is often more than a step needs. The workflow already divides the work, and each step is a scoped run of the CLI. A step that does not delegate, or must not, loses nothing with a minimal toolset and saves those tokens on every call. A broad, open-ended task can still gain from subagents that explore in a separate context.

To compare like with like, we also captured aictrl with only pi's four tools, denying the other five through its permission config. Its first request fell from 3,442 to 2,091 tokens: 608 for the system prompt and 1,421 for the tools. That is 815 tokens above pi, 812 of them in longer descriptions of the same four tools. The run also showed that our system prompt and tool descriptions still mention Task , Glob and Grep when those tools are removed, which we are fixing.

To run aictrl with the same four tools, add these denials to the permission settings in aictrl.json or in the AICTRL_CONFIG_CONTENT environment variable. A denied tool is left out of the request:

{ "permission": { "glob": "deny", "grep": "deny", "task": "deny", "webfetch": "deny", "skill": "deny" } }

Most workflow steps are short, and there the fixed cost per call dominates. In a second scenario each CLI read three 340-byte files and answered, four model calls in all. Every call resends the system prompt, the tool definitions and the history so far.
